title: Learn Before You Buy: Previews, Critics Night & Opening Night - How Your Ticket May Shape a Show!
transcript: There’s a basic question I get all the time. What’s the difference between critics’ night, a preview performance, and opening night? Most people are surprised to learn critics do not review opening night performances. We’re invited earlier during designated press performances, which usually take place near the end of the preview period. My colleagues and I agree to an embargo and hold our reviews until a specific time, just after the official opening. Previews, the performances before opening night, remain a critical part of a show’s development. Although the way they’re used has evolved. During previews, the show continues to be developed in front of a live audience. Performances continue to settle. Technical elements are refined, pacing adjusted, and audience response still matters because actors need a live audience to understand timing, rhythm, energy, and where, hopefully, applause unexpectedly breaks. That said, the show is often close to being complete by that point. In the past, many major changes happened during previews, and audiences would pay less for those pre-opening tickets. Today, shows are usually more fully formed in rehearsal spaces before they even reach the stage. And so, ticket prices are not reduced for those early performances. And by the time critics are invited, the shows are typically frozen. Directors generally won’t allow critics to attend until the work is ready to be judged. Another part of previews audiences don’t always see is how houses are filled. Shows need full audiences to function properly, and producers may give tickets away to insider groups and members of theatrical unions. It is a practice that is known as papering, and it helps to make sure that actors are playing to a full house. This entire system is relatively recent; inviting critics before opening night began in the 1970s. Before that, critics could only attend on opening night. And then they had to rush their reviews to meet same-night newspaper deadlines. My mother, who was a columnist, used to tell me about the stampede of critics racing out to pay phones to make print that night. And that’s why critics traditionally are seated on the aisle. So, when you’re deciding when to buy tickets, it helps to know what you’re walking into. The closer to opening, the more likely you’ll see the polished version. But if you attend an early performance, you can always say you witnessed a show being born.
